We examine the fundamental momentum operators linked to Killing vectors that are both Killing and have tangent paths which are geodesics. Our analysis demonstrates that for any such vector, the corresponding fundamental momentum operator remains Hermitian.

Diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable success in various statistical inference tasks. In the context of Hubbard sign flips, a core challenge in finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo simulations, these models typically face the "sign dilemma": while they excel at representing high-temperature, sign-stable systems, performance degrades significantly as temperatures lower and extensive sign changes occur. This study introduces an innovative dual-network strategy designed to overcome such limitations. The method partitions the lattice into regions containing an even or odd number of sign changes, processing each through a separate neural network. We find that this "sign-flip dual network" achieves optimal results across diverse test cases, including spinless fermions on square and Kagome lattices, as well as electrons experiencing both repulsive and attractive Coulomb interactions.

We examine composite models featuring a single light Higgs boson and two distinct sets of fermions, where one set constitutes the Standard Model (SM) and the other forms a doublet under SM SU(2) gauge symmetry. These second-generation fermions bind to produce the flavon responsible for spontaneous symmetry breaking. This mechanism generates tree-level Yukawa couplings for SM quarks, offering a solution to the hierarchy problem while providing a testable structure for experimental verification.

Virtual Reality (VR) has become a pivotal tool for investigating how the brain constructs perception. Research indicates that VR can be used to alter sensory experiences, yet the perceptual shifts triggered by VR devices themselves are often overlooked. This study introduces a novel framework to explore the "shadow side" of such alterations, specifically examining VR-induced visual field constriction. By utilizing a Virtual Vision Tunnel (VVT) alongside questionnaires and objective metrics, we assessed whether induced field narrowing impacts spatial navigation and mood. Results demonstrated that VR navigation involves more than mere 360-degree scene exploration; it includes active tunnel navigation within the VVT, during which users exhibited increased anxiety and a diminished sense of personal agency. These findings suggest that perceptual modifications caused by VR headsets can significantly influence spatial behavior and emotional states, with important implications for VR applications in clinical settings.

The BigScience Multilingual Framework introduced a collection of multilingual models covering 21 languages and 111 dialects, trained on 1.3 terabytes of data. This study extends that work by adapting the framework for additional languages, specifically Kazakh and Uzbek. We introduce a new multilingual model framework that supports these new linguistic additions.

Fragmentation events involving massive cores that gain rotational speed during their evolution can yield dual systems containing both black holes or dual stellar binaries. By applying a 1D model to simulate a parent core with rising mass and acceleration, we investigate the resulting two-body masses across various initial conditions and acceleration profiles. We observe that rising acceleration can produce dual systems where the mass ratio is less than unity, even if the parent core's final mass exceeds the critical threshold of approximately 100 solar masses ($M_\odot$). Furthermore, we note that increasing the rate of mass gain elevates the lower component's mass within the resulting pair. When applied to current Population III star formation theories, these findings suggest that dual black hole systems may emerge with lower-mass members, even in scenarios where direct collapse into a single black hole is otherwise probable.

We introduce a new method called MArkov Autonomous component KFast analysis (AR-KFAC), which is designed to efficiently and effectively identify the key features of time series data without the need for manual intervention. Unlike traditional supervised learning techniques, our approach builds on recent advancements in unsupervised learning for sequential data, specifically leveraging second-order learning algorithms, precise feature whitening, and stable autonomous learning rules to derive robust components. These elements are then integrated into a secondary hierarchical framework to further enhance the discovered structures. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks, including the popular financial dataset, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both identifying meaningful patterns and forecasting future outcomes.

This paper addresses the complexity of distinguishing labeled diagrams within finite structures, a central issue in finite model theory with significant implications for descriptive complexity. We focus on two specific logics: Choiceless Polynomial Time with Counting (CPTW) and Choiceless Polynomial Time with Duration (CPTWd). Our primary contribution is a separation result demonstrating that while CPTW cannot distinguish certain diagram pairs, CPTWd can. This achievement is the first to identify problems solvable by CPTWd that remain unsolvable by CPTW, thereby validating the increased expressive power of the logic involving duration.

To achieve this, we employ a combination of techniques. First, we establish a connection between the distinguishing capabilities of these diagrams under CPTWd and the ability to resolve specific equivalence questions using the extended polynomial calculus with obligations (EPCO). Second, we establish a correspondence between EPCO refutations of such diagrams and the existence of a "witnessing strategy" for one diagram relative to the other. Leveraging this link, we identify diagrams that constitute a separation for CPTWd versus CPTW. Our future work plans to provide an explicit CPTWd algorithm for distinguishing these specific cases, with the hope that this approach will yield a direct, constructive proof of the difference between the two logics.

Although assertion generation has been extensively investigated, assertions remain a critical component for enhancing software quality. Our primary objective is to autonomously create assertions for Java programs lacking them. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of the Exploring for Framework (JMFPEX), which integrates a mutation-based testing strategy with the execution of exploring operations. Our empirical results demonstrate that the tool significantly outperforms comparable approaches in terms of assertion coverage, successfully generating more valid assertions per line of code than previous methods.

Event detection, which involves locating and categorizing events within text, is crucial for analyzing real-time social media data to identify sudden occurrences. However, detecting events in real time using this method is extremely difficult due to the chaotic nature of social platform content, which often contains irrelevant posts unrelated to an occurrence. This study proposes a new approach to identify events in real time by utilizing time and location data from geotagged social networks. The methodology involves two main components: (1) a retrieval system that gathers relevant, time- and location-tagged data to filter out noise, and (2) a dual-phase processing mechanism. This mechanism first extracts entities, relations, and topics from the filtered data, then performs event identification by analyzing these extracted features. The authors evaluated the method using real-time Twitter streams related to the 2016 US Presidential Elections, demonstrating its capability to identify events efficiently in real time with a reduced reliance on vast amounts of unlabeled data.

Cross-correlating the CMB with large-scale structure (LSS) offers a vital method for probing how primordial fluctuations evolve and are modified throughout cosmic history. This paper introduces a swift technique for generating LSS realizations via Gaussian random fields and applies this through LSS simulations distorted by the CMB. This approach allows for the efficient calculation of the Bispectrum, which examines non-Gaussian characteristics of LSS independent of redshift. We demonstrate the method's validity by correlating our results with those from N-body simulations, showing strong consistency in the LSS–CMB convergence, redshift estimation, and the power spectrum. Furthermore, we find that the method accurately recovers the true bispectrum, with any residual discrepancies falling within statistical error margins.

A significant challenge in machine learning involves ensuring that a trained model maintains trustworthiness when presented with unexpected inputs. While recent research has primarily sought to discover optimization objectives that are provably robust against specific perturbations, this study demonstrates that standard Bayesian learning already provides guaranteed resilience. Specifically, we prove that for any conceivable perturbation type, a Bayesian posterior can be adjusted by a calculable scaling factor to mathematically assure a bounded level of trustworthiness. Empirical results indicate that this inherent guarantee holds strong even with minimal modifications to the prior distributions.

Digital rumors have severely disrupted China's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines the dissemination mechanisms and influence of these rumors on WeChat, China's most widely used social media platform. By analyzing WeChat's hierarchical structure, the authors identified its core hubs and revealed a dissemination pattern driven primarily by strong ties rather than weak ones. The data indicates that digital rumors typically originate within specific professional circles, such as medical, government, or educational sectors, before spreading broadly to the general public. Furthermore, the researchers assessed the impact of these rumors by analyzing the emotional tone of related news reports. Results show a significant negative correlation: the more intense the presence of rumors, the more adverse the sentiment in news coverage.

Unsupervised hyperspectral pixel categorization is a highly intricate challenge, particularly within regions exhibiting significant heterogeneity. While numerous dimensionality reduction techniques have been explored to address this issue, UnSupervised Spectral Dimensionality Minimization (USDM) stands out as a unique approach. This study examines the effects of USDM on hyperspectral pixel categorization, focusing on its capacity to capture both spatial and spectral characteristics. The investigation proceeds in two phases: first, USDM is assessed against established reduction methods regarding dimensionality, classification accuracy, and the specific extraction of spatial and spectral information. Subsequently, USDM's impact on heterogeneous areas is analyzed through a comparison of categorization outcomes in both uniform and diverse zones. The results indicate that USDM effectively enhances classification performance in heterogeneous areas by successfully modeling the relationships between spectral features and spatial- spectral interactions.

We introduce a methodology for deriving natural language frameworks through the reduction of prior frameworks, offering a unifying perspective on existing frame problems and suggesting additional applications.

X-ray crystallography and NMR are the primary experimental methods for determining the 3D structures of proteins and other biomolecules. Once established, these experimental data points are utilized as restraints to generate valid molecular frameworks through energy minimization processes. However, a common issue arises when the number of these restraints is insufficient, leading to a lack of structural convergence or high energy states in the resulting models. This study introduces a new approach that leverages amide proton chemical displacements to produce high-quality structural frameworks. By utilizing quantum mechanical calculations, we derived a comprehensive dataset of approximately 100,000 chemical displacements for various amino acids across different dihedral angles, covering both solvent and bulk environments. This dataset allows us to estimate proton chemical displacements for any specific dihedral angle within a protein. We integrated these estimated values as additional restraints into the energy minimization process for structural framework generation. Experimental validation using NMR and X-ray data confirmed that this method significantly improves structural quality by effectively limiting conformational search spaces. Furthermore, we observed that the resulting frameworks exhibit dihedrals highly consistent with those predicted by quantum physics calculations.

The loss function is integral to deep learning classification tasks, as it quantifies prediction error and guides the optimization of network parameters toward minimizing this discrepancy. Historically, cross-entropy loss has been the standard for image classification due to its efficacy. However, recent investigations have explored various modifications to cross-entropy, including pseudo-entropy, which addresses limitations in handling prediction uncertainty, and the recently introduced label smoothing cross-entropy, which enhances model robustness against noisy training data. This study evaluates these alternative loss functions across three distinct datasets: the ImageNet-12 subset of ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and the Stanford Dogs dataset (often referred to as Dog). Specifically, we examine the impact of pseudo-entropy and label smoothing on the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks. Our findings indicate that both cross-entropy and pseudo-entropy yield comparable classification accuracy, whereas the experimental results demonstrate that altering the loss function through techniques like pseudo-entropy can enhance generalization performance on certain datasets.

The primary objective of this work is to examine parquet theory within a Hamiltonian framework. We establish a parquet-type self-consistent equation for the four-point correlation function, utilizing general principles from the Heisen equation of motion, perturbation theory, and the analysis of perturbative and non-perturbative expansions. The study explicitly constructs the perturbation series for the four-point function up to third order in the Hamiltonian, with the lowest order relying exclusively on projection operators onto eigenstates of the unperturbed system. Furthermore, we incorporate a closure approximation to transform this series into a self-consistent equation. The applicability of parquet theory in the context of the Hubbard model is also explored.

The excitonic phase transition in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) is investigated using *ab initio* many-body techniques. This study details the progress of these methods and their application to the single-layer TMD monolayer, lead-iodide perovskite, and lead-bismuth sulfide, alongside discussion of future research directions.

Urban environments are increasingly vulnerable to escalating crime rates, which severely impact residents' psychological well-being and quality of life. To mitigate these issues, numerous municipalities have adopted smart city technologies, including integrated systems that connect security personnel with dispatchers to enhance public safety. A critical component of such systems involves a text-based interface enabling dispatchers to issue directives to users for crime prevention. However, because these systems operate within closed communities, the underlying data remains inaccessible to external researchers. This paper introduces a data-driven methodology designed to uncover concealed patterns in dispatcher communications by analyzing the linguistic features used when addressing different types of individuals. Specifically, the study employs Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) to automatically classify the recipients of these messages. The proposed classification model utilizes various extracted features to discern distinct communication styles toward specific user groups. Furthermore, the research uncovers significant variations in how dispatchers interact with users based on gender and age, revealing nuanced insights into the interpersonal dynamics of community safety operations.

We examine a superconducting state characterized by p-wave pairing and nematic symmetry breaking. In this regime, the superfluid density varies according to the magnetic field's direction, producing distinct magnetization behaviors for both spin Zeeman and external magnetic field responses, specifically under the assumption of Pauli paramagnetism for triplet Couper pairs. We analyze the system's free energy to the fourth order in order parameter amplitude, noting that this free energy exhibits nematic symmetry. Consequently, the resulting magnetization displays both nematic and polar features, with the latter depending on the orientation of the applied spin field. Furthermore, we investigate how the magnetic field responds to an external field oriented along different crystallographic directions. These findings are supported by analytical considerations of the free energy and verified through numerical simulations.

Engagement serves as a vital component of education, as elevated engagement levels correlate strongly with diminished delinquency, lower absenteeism, and heightened academic performance. This paper introduces a novel framework termed "minimax engaged education" (MEE), designed to enhance student engagement by harmonizing educational content with instructional strategies. The MEE model posits that educators should Minimize the gap between provided learning materials and student interests while simultaneously Maximizing potential engagement levels. To achieve this, we develop a Minimax Engaged Education (MEE) approach that utilizes a multi-view autoencoder to identify latent interest profiles and a minimax optimization algorithm to determine optimal teaching methods based on those interests. Additionally, we constructed the SEI dataset by gathering semi-structured data from Baidu Zhidao, a prominent Chinese Q&A platform, featuring over 1.2 million entries of teacher-student interactions. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed MEE method substantially boosts engagement levels compared to existing approaches.

This study examines power spectra and entropy across varying time scales to evolve data complexity for audio recordings of classical piano pieces, identifying a universal evolution pattern that mirrors the lifecycle of Western classical music. By applying entropy analysis to the fractal dimension of phase space, we associate complexity levels with specific historical epochs, from the Middle Ages through the 20th century. Distinctive complexity signatures for each era are detected, and the resulting entropy evolution aligns with prior scholarly assessments of stylistic shifts. Furthermore, these findings demonstrate the utility of entropy as a diagnostic tool for identifying temporal markers in digital audio.

The reinforcement method, first introduced by Laplace in 1818, serves as a foundational mechanism for addressing problems in probability theory. This paper examines a generalization of the Bernoulli coin-throwing process featuring multiple sides, in which the outcome probabilities are unknown. This model represents an extension of the original two-outcome scenario first studied by Laplace in 1812 and was later formalized by Rhee and Rhee in 2018 for a two-branch case. The current work investigates the asymptotic properties of a reinforcement scheme applicable to an $n$-branch system, where each branch is assigned a prior weight. The findings demonstrate that the long-term behavior of the procedure yields an asymptotically optimal universal testing framework, effectively extending the results achieved by Rhee and Rhee to a domain with multiple outcomes.

This study investigates how to create light-based harmony through gameplay, blending computational aesthetics with artistic harmony. It defines aesthetic harmony as a computational concept and introduces a playful, harmony-based illumination system driven by a harmony calculator. This core component translates musical intervals into harmony values, which the game utilizes to generate pleasing lighting effects. To ensure the gaming experience remains enjoyable, playful elements are integrated alongside the harmonic mechanics. Ultimately, the research evaluates this system by examining its artistic and recreational impacts, discussing both the potential benefits and limitations of integrating harmony into interactive play.

Reward learning has emerged as a vital component for enabling end-to-end training of deep learning models in autonomous driving. However, existing methods often struggle with the subjective nature of reward construction, relying heavily on costly human annotators who must evaluate every training frame. Furthermore, these approaches fail to leverage the potential of post-training human evaluation to enhance model performance. To address these limitations, we introduce a visually assisted cluster-ranking method that eliminates the need for continuous human annotation during training while maximizing the utility of human input after initial model generation. By facilitating direct human feedback on specific image clusters and accelerating the reinforcement process through effective integration of that input, we demonstrate through experiments on the nuScenes dataset that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

We demonstrate that Smyth power space over a core-compact domain, when subjected to the concisely ordered topology, possesses the property of core-compactness. Furthermore, we show that this property holds if, and only if, it equates to the lattice of all non-empty closed subsets equipped with the lower Vietoris topology.

It is worth noting that this result corrects a previous claim by Dijkstra and Thijssen, who asserted in their 1988 work that the same equivalence applied to the Scott topology. Our analysis reveals that the Dijkstra and Thijssen assertion for the Scott topology is actually inaccurate.

This study investigates loop vortex dynamics in a perfectly planar, delta-function repulsive repulsive vortex-vortex interaction system. We find that the system's energy is minimized when the loop radius matches the interaction length scale, $R_{\text{loop}} = \ell$. Consequently, an aimed loop—defined as one where the center of vorticity aligns with the vortex line—is shown to be unstable, spontaneously breaking into two co-rotating point vortices situated on opposite sides of the line. This instability arises because the system lowers its energy by elongating the loop; during this contraction, the orbiting frequency of the resulting pair increases. As this frequency rises indefinitely as the loop approaches zero radius, it diverges to infinity in a limit of vanishing size. Ultimately, the continuous emission of waves during the contraction process accounts for the loop's disintegration.

This study introduces SEDI LW, a standardized approach to inverse likelihood weighting that utilizes a neural network to forecast the influence of the inverse likelihood. The method addresses a critical limitation in traditional I LW: the excessive variance caused by extreme values of the influence function, which negatively impacts both out-of-sample forecast accuracy and computational performance. The proposed neural network is trained on historical data to predict this influence function, enabling its application to future out-of-sample periods. The paper evaluates SEDI LW against several alternatives, including standard historical simulation, conditional VaR, conditional-conditional VaR, and multiple weighted backtesting techniques, across three distinct financial datasets.

The paper presents a theoretical analysis of recent measurements polarized proton production cross sections, which utilize these datasets to determine the polarized $\tau$-nucleon asymmetry. This particle's decay asymmetry offers a unique probe for testing the V-A structure of the weak interaction, a capability that has been hindered by the need for precise knowledge of the proton polarization and the target's spin-dependent parton distribution functions. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of the experimental requirements and associated theoretical challenges, specifically addressing the impact of charm quark production on the extracted asymmetries.

This study presents a comprehensive experimental and computational analysis of a rotating annulus driven by horizontal temperature differences across end walls, conducted under zero relative vorticity conditions. The experiments utilized a high-resolution particle image velocimetry (PIV) system to measure both mean and fluctuating velocity fields, while the numerical simulations employed the spectral element method. The investigation focused on a specific benchmark case involving a large aspect ratio of 10 and a large Rossby number of 0.1, allowing for a direct comparison between observed data and simulated results. The primary objective was to evaluate the capability of the used computational model in replicating the physical dynamics of the observed flow. The analysis revealed that the model accurately captured the generation of baroclinic waves, their subsequent merging into the basic state, the development of axisymmetric instabilities, the formation of mean zonal flow, and the statistical characteristics of the wave fluctuations. Furthermore, the simulations successfully modeled the transition from wave-dominated regimes to quasi-geostrophic states as the rotation rate decreased. The authors conclude that the employed model is a valuable tool for simulating the dynamics within rotating fluids.

We introduce a new parametrization of the Poisson process used to count exceedances above high thresholds, offering a unified framework for the threshold-dependent measure and the limiting process characterized by the Generalized Pareto scheme. While maintaining flexibility for non-stationary exceedance behaviors, this approach facilitates the computation of extreme quantiles and Value-at-Risk estimates alongside the derivation of necessary inferential tools for Bayesian implementation. Its utility and performance are demonstrated through applications to both simulated data and real-world examples.

Recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning (RL) have yielded impressive results across numerous domains, including robotics, gaming, and autonomous driving. However, the black-box nature of these AI systems renders them highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can corrupt the reward signals, leading to severe outcomes like compromised self-driving vehicles or robotic failures. To address this, Corruption-Resilient Learning (CRL) seeks to enable RL agents to recognize and adapt to malicious reward perturbations despite the inherent difficulty of separating attack noise from genuine environmental feedback. While most CRL research focuses on online learning scenarios, real-world deployments typically involve pre-training agents on vast historical datasets before deployment, often without continuous access to the environment. This paper introduces **Offset CRL**, a novel offline approach designed to extract robust, corruption-neutral policies from historical data. The method first calculates the causal offset between states and rewards to filter out malicious noise, subsequently training a value function and an agent using distributionally robust MDPs and behavior cloning. Demonstrated through extensive simulations in both continuous and discrete environments, the results confirm that Offset CRL significantly outperforms existing offline methods in resilience against corrupted rewards.

This paper investigates the heat equation on a one-dimensional domain with variable boundary conditions, focusing on exact boundary controllability for temperature and its heat flux. The study analyzes two distinct scenarios: the first involves smooth impulsive heat supply or extraction, while the second addresses situations where such impulses occur without smooth transitions. For the third case, a new concept termed logarithmic curvature is introduced to characterize the smooth spatial variation of the heat supply or demand. Specifically, when this curvature is negative, the problem corresponds to focusing supply, whereas positive curvature relates to extraction. The analysis demonstrates that impulsive control is viable for both temperature regulation and the simultaneous stabilization of temperature and flux only within domains where this logarithmic curvature maintains a consistent sign. Furthermore, for the smooth impulsive strategy to be applicable, a specific relationship must exist between the logarithmic curvature and the desired final distribution of temperature and heat supply.

Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection is a critical area within machine learning, with applications ranging from automated content moderation to medical diagnosis. Although the majority of existing OOD detection research relies on image data, the current study addresses the challenge using text inputs. We introduce a taxonomy of three primary OOD text categories: (1) domain-oOD, which targets text from different domains than the training material, (2) concept-OOD, which consists of text unrelated to the training concepts, and (3) in-context concept-OOD, which includes text unrelated to training data that appears among in-context examples in few-shot settings. We find that standard techniques relying on distributional assumptions fail to detect in-context concept-OOD otext. To address this, we propose a new method that utilizes the structural properties of in-context concept-OOD to achieve detection. Experiments across multiple datasets and various tasks validate the effectiveness of our proposed solution.

Brownian molecular engines, which derive their power from inelastic electron tunneling, have attracted significant interest for their potential in nanoscale thermal energy conversion. Despite this attention, a rigorous theoretical framework describing their operation has been lacking. In response, we present a dynamical model that integrates Tersoff-Hamann-based dynamics with the non-equilibrium Keldysh Green's function formalism. This approach enables the computation of both the system's time-dependent evolution and steady-state properties, specifically the probability distribution of the rotor, current-voltage characteristics, and the efficiency of heat-to-electricity conversion. Furthermore, we examine how the engine's performance and underlying probability distributions are influenced by temperature, the spatial extension of the probe tip, and the chemical potential window.

Term transducers serve as a generalization of both resynchronization devices like synchronous and monosynchronous dual-mode word transducers, as well as relationally defined mappings used in computer science. Within this framework, the concept of synchronization has been broadened to cover pairs of binary term mappings. A key property for these devices is resynchronization, which ensures that input terms map to corresponding output terms at regular intervals. The study presented here concentrates on unidirectional term transducers, a subclass where transformation rules are strictly left-to-right. The authors demonstrate that for these devices, resynchronization can be expected only in an asymmetric, one-way sense. Specifically, they prove this assumption holds true for a significant subset of unidirectional devices: those capable of simulating relations derived from finite index sets. The paper further establishes that these directional devices can be effectively converted into a specific type of limit-state automaton operating on bi-nary terms.

This paper introduces a novel, high-performance algorithm for computing generalized convolutions more rapidly than traditional brute force methods. While the approach maintains compatibility with various generalizations, it offers specific enhancements for standard convolution operations.

The discovery of the T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 marked a turning point in the field of exoplanets, as it was the first brown dwarf identified with a distinctively T-type spectral classification. Although subsequent spectral surveys have largely concentrated on the M-dwarf regime, this study utilizes the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze the full spectral range of GJ 229B (1.0–24.0 μm) to evaluate the current understanding of T-dwarf atmospheres. Our analysis indicates that the atmosphere is clear, showing no evidence of clouds or hazes, and that the object possesses a low surface gravity. The derived physical parameters are an effective temperature of 670 ± 20 K, a surface gravity of log(g) = 4.7 ± 0.3 (cgs), and a mass of 0.032 ± 0.004 M_Jup. The study also addresses the origin of the prominent 11.3 μm gap in the spectral energy distribution, proposing that it arises from a combination of the intrinsic opacity gap in the silicate doublet and the presence of water vapor absorption. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that the APOLLO code is highly effective for modeling the spectra of T-dwarfs.

This document details the methodologies employed by the LHCb collaboration in analyzing Bs meson decays into J/psi pi0 and J/psi eta. The study utilizes data from 3.0 fb-1 of proton-proton collisions collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The analysis leverages the full 2012 dataset, combining 2010 and 2011 runs, which includes 6012 and 4000 events respectively. The analysis focuses on the extraction of the semileptonic branching ratio and the determination of the width difference between the B_s^0 and B_s^1 states. The results are presented in the context of the Standard Model predictions and previous experimental measurements.

This study evaluates the utility of well-mixed and spatially explicit frameworks for forecasting infections and valuing related policy interventions within urban bus environments. We begin by formulating a well-mixed model to estimate the baseline spread of infections on buses, subsequently addressing the limitations of this approach by developing a spatially explicit framework that incorporates infection dynamics across an urban transit network. We then compare both modeling methods to determine their respective policy values, focusing on forecasting accuracy and the optimization of contact-tracing strategies. The results indicate that well-mixed framework policies are nearly as effective as those derived from spatially explicit models, suggesting that simpler well-mixed frameworks are sufficient for creating cost-infectious policy interventions targeting urban bus users.

This study employs the shell-model to investigate prohibited beta-decay properties of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te, focusing on the transitions to $^{135,137}$I. The wave functions utilized were generated using the GXPF1A interaction, with matrix elements for the unique particle-hole operator $\hat{R}_{\mu}^{\pm}$ computed via the cranking method. Theoretical predictions for log $ft$ values associated with first-forbidden non-unique (1$f_{\nu u}$) one- and two-step processes align well with corresponding experimental measurements. Additionally, the wave function analysis indicates that the particle holes in $^{135,137}$I are situated in the $1g_{9/2}$ shell, while the particle in $^{135,137}$I resides in the $2d_{5/2}$ shell.

The rise of the Internet has enabled the growth of online brokerages, facilitating the trading of goods and services across global markets. These platforms, however, introduce significant challenges related to authentication and trust. This paper introduces a solution utilizing digital certificates for authentication within electronic double-sided auction systems. The proposed framework ensures transparent and fair trading by employing digital-certificate-secured communication, specifically tailored for markets dealing with financial assets.

Utilizing the heavy quark effective theory (HQET), we have calculated the bottom- and top-favored semileptonic decay f-wave mesons bottom to top. In this work, we examine the f-wave bottom to top transition. In the kinematic region of zero momentum transfer, we obtain V=0.29 and A_1=0.29. In the kinematic region of zero recoil, we obtain R=0.29.

We investigate the optimization of a specific class of nonexpansive path lengths connecting two fixed points within a given domain. This investigation centers on a periodic composition involving a given function and the "max" operator. The study examines both the continuous framework and its discrete approximation through the algorithm known as the max-plus Jacobi iteration. We establish the convergence of this approximation and demonstrate that the optimal value found discretely approaches the continuous optimum with a relative error decaying quadratically. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound for this continuous optimal value using a technique inspired by the "min-plus" genre of tropical geometry.

The demand for real-time analysis of high-dimensional time series data has driven the development of rapid dimensionality reduction techniques. Among these, Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) and its nonlinear extension, Nonlinear DMD (nDMD), are widely utilized for identifying temporal patterns in complex systems. However, both methods typically require extensive human expertise to interpret results and manage potential model failures, such as aliasing or overfitting. This study introduces Kernel DMD (kDMD) and Nonlinear DMD (nkDMD) as robust alternatives capable of handling large-scale, real-time datasets effectively. The proposed frameworks employ kernel techniques to enhance interpretability and resilience, specifically addressing the limitations of overfitting and aliasing. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that the new models successfully detect meaningful temporal dynamics while maintaining robustness.

This paper introduces a novel metric for evaluating the similarity of chess openings, grounded in a graph representation of the openings ecosystem. We demonstrate this metric's effectiveness in quantifying the complexity of specific opening lines and assessing the relationship between distinct chess openings.

Pale dwarfs are anticipated to host millisecond pulsars (MSPs) resulting from recycled millisecond pulsations formed within close binary systems. Detecting these pale dwarfs is expected to yield the discovery of new MSPs, thereby enabling the determination of their physical characteristics. This study introduces a novel technique for identifying candidate pale dwarfs by applying the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to the light curves of pulsating stars. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method using the well-established pulsating star sample from the OGLE-III survey. Furthermore, we outline the procedures for characterizing discovered candidates and conclude that this approach offers a valuable asset for the OGLE-IV project.

This work examines the motion characteristics of arbitrary finite systems described by a conservative framework, utilizing characterizations of both linear and angular momentum alongside a generalized form of energy. Notably, these definitions hold true regardless of the order of the Euler-Lagrange differential equations involved.

Immersive Virtual Reality (VR) environments are increasingly recognized for their ability to facilitate human-Computer Interaction (HCI) in creating, modifying, and interpreting three-dimensional (3D) forms. This study introduces a new HCI approach for VR 2D/3D sketching that supports free rotation around the X, Y, and Y axes, utilizing hand gestures to define gestures for specific axis manipulations. VR sketches generated through this method can be converted into 3D models by integrating sketches from multiple viewpoints, serving as input for retrieving similar models from a database. To validate this, the VR interface was assessed for sketching efficiency and accuracy, and the resulting 3D formation process was evaluated by measuring retrieval performance using the Mean Average Precision (MAP) metric.

The upcoming James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) will possess significantly greater sensitivity than its predecessors, enabling it to characterize the atmospheres of small, rocky exoplanets. However, the lack of precise ephemerides for these systems poses a significant challenge to conducting such studies. This study introduces a new methodology to enhance ephemerides by leveraging a global network of amateur telescopes. We demonstrate the approach using a planet exhibiting particularly large orbital eccentricity, HD 80606 b. By analyzing a decade of data from a worldwide array of amateur observatories, we achieved a reduction in orbital uncertainty by a factor of 100. Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of timing errors on JWST scheduling, revealing that current precision is insufficient for critical atmospheric studies. To address this, we developed a correction algorithm that refines prediction accuracy to the minute level.

This paper examines the Feasasibility of isentropic ideal fluid collapse governed by a linear equation of states, P = K\rho. The analysis demonstrates that a static configuration remains statically stable if it adheres to the surface integral condition \int_0^R \frac{\rho_c}{\rho} j_0(\frac{\chi r}{R}) dr > 0, where R denotes the star's radius, \rho_c represents the central density, and the remaining terms involve Bessel function components. Furthermore, it proves that initiating a dynamic collapse from any static state is always possible under these conditions.

We employ the Iyer-Wald formalism to revisit extremal black hole solutions within a general theory of gravity characterized by an arbitrary fall-off term linking surface area and mass. Our analysis reveals that, for charged extremal black holes, this specific thermodynamic framework mandates a zero spin-coefficient derivative across the entire event horizon—a condition we validate using the Einstein-Maxwell system. Additionally, within this framework, we demonstrate that the mass of an extremal black hole hole equates to one-half the mass derivative with respect to its horizon area, a relationship holding universally under general theories of gravity. Finally, we apply this broad theoretical approach to the EMDR (Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-Charged) black hole scenario.

Recent studies indicate that input features within deep neural networks (DNNs) often retain significant utility near the output layer, even after passing through multiple pooling and convolutional operations. Building on this, the authors propose the End-Influence Investigation (EII) metric to measure how final layers respond to inputs, specifically highlighting the sensitivity to distinct regions of the input space. EII serves a dual purpose: it acts as a reliable tool for hyperparameter optimization and acts as an indicator of efficient engine learning. The study demonstrates that pooling strategies which maximize end-influence facilitate more effective training, particularly for image recognition tasks.

We introduce a Poincaré symmetry-based framework for (anti-)self-dual gravity in four dimensions, extending the vibrant Poincaré symmetry concept previously applied to general relativity. This extended formalism treats (anti-)self-dual gravitational potentials as components of a vibrant connection on a principal $GL^+(2,\mathbb{C})$ bundle, distinguished by a specific self-adjoint gauge field. This gauge field functions as a metric, which can be dynamically linked to a real scalar field through a kinetic term. This mechanism mirrors an existing proposal for the (anti-)self-dual parts of an auxiliary metric in type IIB supergravity, where that metric is derived from the squared absolute values of the scalar axion-dilaton field. Furthermore, we propose a corresponding particle model based on vibrant symmetry, offering an alternative to the standard Weyl doublet by utilizing a single scalar field alongside a kinetic term that enforces an invariant mass.

An upward planar drawing of a directed graph assigns positions to its nodes and edges such that no edges cross and all paths move strictly vertically higher. Determining whether an arbitrary network admits such a drawing is an NP-complete challenge. This research investigates the problem through parameterized complexity, initially establishing a cubic kernel for graphs parameterized by feedback vertex set size. This finding implies the problem is FPT. Furthermore, the study presents a solution achieving XP time complexity when using bidirectedness as a parameter and confirms that recognizing upward planar bidirected graphs can be done in linear time.

This paper examines the evolution of compact base stations (BSs) from the fourth generation (4G) through projected fifth-generation (6G) networks. It begins by analyzing the historical background of the compact cell concept and its advantages, followed by a review of the present state of small- and micro-macro systems. The authors further explore the potential trajectory of the compact cell for next-generation (6G) networks, highlighting the roles of compact macro cells and the integrated network. Key future research challenges are identified, specifically focusing on the coexistence of compact and conventional cells, the impact of compact cells on network topology, and the effects of their deployment on energy efficiency.

Current research into social dynamics frequently relies on hypergraph models, which allow edges to connect any subset of nodes rather than being restricted to pairs. This paper introduces a new framework for dynamic hypergraphs that captures the temporal evolution of both the hypergraph structure and the attributes of its nodes. We propose a formalism for a broad class of update mechanisms, demonstrating that for any specific mechanism, there exists an associated linear operator that governs the attribute propagation across a fixed framework. Furthermore, in the case of random dynamic hypergraphs where the structure evolves stochastically while nodes update sequentially, we analyze the resulting propagation effects. Our findings reveal that the update rules dictate the characteristics of the resulting propagations, which we study through both rigorous mathematical theorems and computational simulations.

We investigate how the operator product expansion (OPE) and the scalar-fission integral (SFI) approach interconnect within the context of deep inelastic scattering (DIS). In the SFI method, DIS is analyzed by modeling the hadron as a continuum of partons moving with a light-cone momentum fraction $x$, each possessing transverse momentum $\mathbf{k}_\perp$ and a specific twist structure. By evaluating matrix elements for light-cone distributions (LCDAs) and comparing them with those derived from the OPE framework, we demonstrate that the two approaches inherently address the same underlying physics. Furthermore, we illustrate how the distinct Wilson coefficients within the SIF correspond to those found in the OPE.

The direct decay of $^{16}$Be into an $\alpha$ particle and two neutrons, proceeding from the Hoyle state, offers a vital pathway for investigating alpha-clustering characteristics. This study presents the initial ECT experiment, which directly observed this specific three-body reaction. By analyzing the angular distribution of the emitted triton and $\alpha$ particle, researchers have determined the reaction's differential cross-section. The findings indicate that the derived differential cross-sections align well with theoretical models, notably the resonant-state approximation and the R-matrix formalism. Furthermore, the measured angular distribution supports a value of the reduced decay matrix element, $|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}|^2$, of approximately 0.77 fm$^4$, which is consistent with recent theoretical predictions.

This study investigates oscillatory and tip-dividing instabilities within two-dimensional dynamic brittle fracture using plane strain conditions and linear elastic fracture mechanics. By analyzing the singular asymptotic fields at the crack tip and employing numerical simulations, we examine how initial energy release rates, oscillatory wave patterns, and branching instabilities evolve. We observe that decreasing the inherent material length scale amplifies the oscillatory instability and diminishes the release rate required for branching to occur. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the temporal scale influences the development of both instabilities. Crack propagation releases are shown to be size-dependent, with results indicating reduced release rate thresholds for oscillatory and branching events as material dimensions decrease.

This work investigates communication over finite-state channels where feedback is available. The channel states exist in a finite non-markovian stochastic environment, and channel output states are observable. Under the assumption of non-causal state knowledge at the encoder, achievable regions are derived for both discrete memoryless sources and those with causal encoding.

This paper investigates superfluidity in two-dimensional cold atoms with Rashba spin-orbit coupling under a square lattice and a global Zeeman field, focusing on the low-density regime where an attractive interaction is present. We analyze both spin-singlet and spin-triplet mechanisms for the resulting superfluidity, employing a combination of weak-coupling many-body theory and numerical simulations. Our weak-coupling analysis reveals that, contrary to the absence of a superfluid transition in the spin-triplet channel within a lattice structure, the spin-singlet pairing can induce a topological superfluid state characterized by a non-zero Chern number. Furthermore, we examine the pairing dynamics in the spin-singlet regime using a variational approach based on the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and mean-field approximation within a Stochastic Mean-field framework.

This paper details our team's (EMLP) approach to SemEval-2021 Task 9, which involved two sub-treatments: (1) identifying and extracting tables from the text of scientific papers, and (2) assessing the veracity of table data. We utilized the table datasets from the PubTabNet collection for the first stage, which allowed us to achieve the top-ten results on the development set and a top-ten finish on the final test set. For the second stage, which entailed verifying table-related claims, we employed a hybrid strategy combining rule-based methods with pre-trained transformer models. This combination yielded the second-best outcome on the competition leaderboard.

In quantum physics, intricate numbers are defined as irrational constants appearing in theory that are theoretically derivable yet empirically undetermined due to measurement limitations. This discussion examines the intricacy of $\xi$, a parameter in the anharmonic oscillator theory linking its zero-point energy to anharmonicity. Introducing a link between the theory of intricate numbers and the Heuristic Universal Power Law (HUP L), we propose a theoretical framework to model the evolution of the universe.

This paper defines and examines a graph-theoretical extension called the shortened distance. For a specified positive integer k, the k-shortened distance between two vertices is the count of edges on the shortest k-path connecting them, where a k-path is a simple path containing no more than k edges. Consequently, the r-dimensional Shortened Breadth for a graph G is the maximal cardinality of a subset of G such that, for every vertex in V(G), its breadth values relative to each member of this subset are distinct when calculated using the respective k-shortened distance metric.
