This study introduces a mechanism explaining how entropy collapses when its potential maximum is approached, observed in both experimental and theoretical systems. We investigate the binary entropy of one-dimensional chaotic maps, specifically focusing on the Mersenne and the newly proposed "negative" logistic maps, which exhibit symmetry under entropy reversal. We propose that heterochaos underlies the emergence of the observed bimodal entropy distribution, characterized by a minimum at zero and a maximum at a non-zero value. To analyze systems exhibiting heterochaos, we developed the Heterochaos Baker Number (HBN), a metric indicating the degree of mixing; values near one signify mixing, while values approaching zero indicate a lack thereof. Furthermore, we constructed a heterochaos-specific algorithm to generate symbolic sequences, enabling the identification of the mechanism responsible for bimodality through an examination of the most probable sequences.

We investigate the prospects for detecting the prolonged Proca scalar, a novel boson featuring extended lifetimes and mass around 125 GeV, at present and future collider facilities. Our analysis demonstrates that the Extended Standard Model, which incorporates this particle, remains consistent with all existing experimental data. We further detail the strategies employed to identify the particle through its decay into $\tau\tau$ and $\gamma Z$ channels, noting that current LHC data already impose significant constraints on its production cross-section. We project that the High-Luminosity LHC will refine these limits by an order of magnitude, while the proposed Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) muon-specific detector could enhance sensitivity by a factor of 100.

The advent of deep learning has significantly advanced text-to-speech (TTS) systems, yet current deep generative models for synthesizing raw audio waves often struggle with slow inference speeds and a lack of pitch controllability. This study introduces Quasi-periodic WaveNet (QP-GAN), a pitch-conditioned wave generation network designed to produce high-fidelity, raw waveform audio at high velocities via autoregressive methods. To enhance both pitch sensitivity and sampling efficiency, the proposed architecture integrates a pitch-conventioned ConvLSTM module alongside pitch-sensitive dilated convolutions. These ConvLSTM and dilated convolution operations utilize network architectures employing skip connections and depth-wise separable convolutions to improve both generation efficiency and model quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that QP-GAN achieves faster generation speeds and higher audio fidelity than the standard WaveNet, while also exhibiting a superior ability to generate pitch-controllable speech.

Collaborative filtering (CF) remains a primary method for addressing the challenges of information overload and uncertainty in finding suitable items for individuals. However, the inherent subjectivity of user preferences, combined with sparsity and the local nature of user-item interactions, significantly limit the effectiveness of traditional collaborative filtering approaches. To overcome these barriers, this paper introduces a novel Bicluster-based CF system enhanced with the users' perspective. By utilizing shared interest groups within the bi-clustering framework, the method mitigates issues arising from data sparsity and preference locality. Furthermore, the system integrates the concept of "preference strength" to refine the selection of relevant users, thereby enhancing the accuracy of item recommendations. Empirical evaluations using two real-world datasets demonstrate that this new method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study utilizes disk-integrated and spectral-line observations from the Sun, acquired by the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) with the HARPS-N instrument, to examine the relationships among the photosphere's magnetic activity, spectral features, and light variations. We specifically investigate magnetic influence on integrated signals and identify novel activity markers by analyzing line-by-line fluxes and broad spectral indices. Our approach combines these datasets with simultaneous photospheric magnetic field measurements from the Vector Spectromagnetometer (VSM), located on the Solar Telescope at the Tenerife observatory. We observe that flux variations in both the visible and near-infrared spectra are strongly correlated with VSM data, with a correlation coefficient of 0.94 at 557.7 nm and 0.89 at 1.01 µm. Furthermore, we investigate the physical mechanisms driving flux changes across the spectrum by modeling solar absorption lines using the radiative transfer code RADIATIVE. These simulations, which incorporate magnetic field parameters from the VSM, successfully reproduce flux variations in both observed bands, with predicted variations of 0.0005 at 557.7 nm and 0.0015 at 1.01 µm.

To effectively distinguish Majorana zero-energy peaks from those arising at non-zero energies, we propose conducting tunneling spectroscopy using superconducting electrodes characterized by Ohmic dissipation (specifically, resistive or "dirtier" electrodes) rather than normal metal ones. In this setup, we demonstrate that the tunning conductance associated with a Majorana zero-energy state follows a linear voltage dependence, whereas signatures from other zero-energy states remain distinct. Conversely, when employing ideal (clean) superconducting electrodes, Majorana conductance is predicted to be a sharp delta function; under these same conditions, we show that tunneling conductance from other non-zero energies also converges to a delta function, thereby eliminating the ability to differentiate between the different peak types.

This research investigates the bicategorical shadow, a generalization of the well-established notion of a bicategorical trace. We establish fundamental properties and provide representations of shadows within the 2-category of 1-categories and pseudo-functors, as well as in the 2-category of -category algebras. A key result demonstrates that the shadow of a bicategory is idempotent, thereby supporting the development of the bicategorical Beck monadicity theorem. Furthermore, the article begins to explore the role of the bicategorical shadow in topological quantum field theory.

Although tone mapping has long been the focus of research, existing methods often fail to replicate the versatile stylistic effects produced by popular commercial software like Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom. To address this, we introduce a novel data-driven approach for extracting stylistic cues from collections of tones-adjusted images. First, our method derives a robust tone representation using the structure-from-motion technique applied to multi-view image datasets. Next, by analyzing pixel-level disparities between standard and processed images within this representation, the model isolates specific stylistic features such as contrast, color balance, and sharpness. Finally, these extracted styles are utilized to enhance both general forward tone mapping and, conversely, reverse tone mapping for the original content. The underlying framework for both applications is trained on large-scale datasets comprising diverse input images and corresponding edited versions. Evaluations conducted on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that the proposed system successfully captures distinct stylistic properties and achieves superior performance in tone mapping tasks when compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

This study introduces the AQTC dataset, which is dedicated to identifying ambiguous questions within customer support ticket documents. The data comprises 1,028 instances drawn from GitHub repositories for various software projects, with each instance featuring a source text, a query based on that text, and a set of three candidate questions for classification as either the original or an ambiguity. The candidates were curated by three domain experts per example to ensure relevance. To evaluate our methods, we employed both baseline approaches and advanced models, ultimately achieving a test F1 score of 0.7003.

This study presents the inaugural rigorous scientific validation of selective light scattering (often called selective sweeping) in snowfall within atmospheric turbulence. Experiments were conducted using a laser scanning vibrometer to measure the transverse velocity of natural atmospheric turbulence combined with high-speed digital imaging to observe snowflakes. The results revealed a lower limit on the size of snowflakes, approximately 2.5 mm, below which the particles exhibit this specific scintillation effect.

We introduce the concept of Self-Governing Navigation (SGN) for robots, defined as the ability to autonomously explore an environment indefinitely without external guidance, relying only on minimal initial human inputs such as basic maps or tutorials. To achieve SGN, a robot must possess the ability to plan paths, learn from them, and generate new skills, all while adapting to dynamic changes in real-world settings. We demonstrate that SGN can be realized through Profound Active Deduction (PAD), a framework that combines logical reasoning with machine learning. Under PAD, a robot maintains both explicit knowledge (e.g., "the red button opens the door") and implicit knowledge (e.g., "the button is located to the left") within its memory, continuously refining its understanding of the world as it gathers new experiences.

The foundation of PAD is an internal World Model that mirrors the robot's understanding, enabling the system to simulate actions and predict their outcomes. By leveraging this simulation capability, the robot can deduce the effects of untried behaviors, thereby navigating complex scenarios and overcoming obstacles for which it was not originally programmed.

Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of PAD across diverse, realistic simulations, including self-driving car scenarios and robotic exploration within hazardous environments like nuclear power plants. These tests confirm that PAD enables robots to navigate their realms and execute intricate tasks, exhibiting a level of autonomy comparable to, or exceeding, that of human operators.

Three-dimensional Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) are a favored detection technology for next-generation dark matter experiments, as they provide ionization trails from interacting particles that span the intensity and temporal resolutions needed to distinguish signals from background noise. Nevertheless, these 3D sparse TPCs generate point cloud data at such high volumes that they risk overwhelming the processing capabilities of even the most advanced computing systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method for efficient TPC point cloud compression that retains critical information while substantially reducing data volume. Our approach employs a bicephalous Convolutional Autoencoder (bCE-3D-GAN), which integrates a Convolutional Autoencoder with an auxiliary discriminator to refine the reconstruction of compressed point clouds. Notably, this architecture allows for self-supervised training without a requirement for ground truth data. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves an effective data reduction of up to 95% with negligible loss in physical information, all while maintaining robust performance in the absence of reference data for training.

The Finzi gravitational model, a relativistic theory of gravitation, has been employed to investigate statistical properties of galaxy clusters. In this study, the spatial distribution of the clusters is modeled using a homogeneous Poisson process, allowing for the derivation of statistical averages for the Finzi model's parameters. The resulting statistical characteristics of the model are subsequently compared against observational data.

A $k$-uniform hypergraph is defined as a set of subsets, each containing $k$ vertices, drawn from a finite ground set $V$. Such a hypergraph is considered convex if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the subsets forming the hypergraph are subsets of the shortest paths (geodesics) connecting $u$ and $v$ within the generated graph structure. This paper establishes that for any uniformity level $k$, the saturation number for convex geometric hypergraphs is $\binom{2k}{k}-1$.

This study introduces a novel theoretical framework for calculating inclusive alpha particle spectra in the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V interaction. The model accounts for the two-body structure of the projectile, treating the emitted alpha particle as a "quasifree" entity resulting from collisions between its constituents and the target, while simultaneously reflecting the nuclear response via the optical potential. Theoretically, high-energy elastic scattering data for the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V system were analyzed using the equivalent collision concept to determine the complex optical potential for an imaginary alpha-$^{6}$Li proxy and a real alpha-probe interacting with the target. The resulting optical potential for a hypothetical imaginary projectile was subsequently transformed into a complex profile for the imaginary component of an alpha-$^{6}$Li equivalent, while the real part was derived via Galilean transformation. The calculated alpha-particle spectra were then generated by convoluting the inclusive cross-section for internal breakup of $^{6}$Li with the elastic scattering angular distribution of an alpha-probe on the target. The derived model successfully reproduces the experimental data for alpha-particle generation across the entire angular range.

This paper introduces a novel approach to neural architecture search (NAS) called PLAGEN, designed to generate a continuous sequence of related neural networks that progressively improve in performance. The core mechanism relies on a motivation system derived from the swimming behaviors of Pacific lampreys, specifically their ability to climb obstacles. By integrating this biological inspiration with a variation of the EVOLVO search algorithm, we can generate each new network architecture based on the successful components of its predecessor while also injecting novel features. Empirical results on the NAS-Bench-201 environment demonstrate that PLAGEN not only rapidly discovers high-performing models but also creates an efficient architectural lineage where each successive design outperforms the last.

This research investigates how ideal treatment strategies impact an immune response against colon cancer by employing a Fokker-Planck model. We begin by formulating a reaction scheme for tumor-immune interaction, which is subsequently simulated using a stochastic finite-difference method to obtain the probability density function (PDF) of cellular concentrations. These concentration levels, represented by the PDF's zero-crossings, are then analyzed through various parameters, specifically focusing on the consequences of applying ideal customized therapies.

This study introduces a deep learning-based scheduling approach for Device-to-Device (D2D) networks, designed to mitigate interferences between D2D links and cellular users (CUs). The proposed algorithm determines the optimal uplink transmission power and resource block (RB) allocation for D2D users, ensuring they do not exceed cellular capacity limits. By modeling RB allocation as a column permutation problem and D2D uplink power as a non-convex optimization challenge, the method employs an autoencoder neural network to generate a compact feature representation. This encoding is followed by the generation of power and RB strategies using the network's decoder. The autoencoder is refined via end-to-end training with the deep Q-learning algorithm. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the method achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art solutions while significantly lowering computational complexity.

We establish that for smooth, compactly supported initial data on periodic domains, the 3D compressible inviscid Euler equations preserve both total and helically broken down kinetic energy, as well as magnetic helicity, for a definite period. Furthermore, leveraging existing $H^s$ ($s$ sufficiently large) a priori bounds for the compressible Euler system, we derive the same smoothness-based a priori estimates for the 3D compressible, magnetized Euler equations when acting on helical periodic initial data. Notably, our time-dependent a priori estimates are distinct from those found in the literature regarding the Navier-Stokes-on-a-chip equations.

The wave systems known as water waves exhibit a wide range of characteristics, including dispersion relations, nonlinear interactions, and wave-wave coupling. To model these phenomena, the Davey-Stewartson equations offer valuable insights. This study examines the scattering behavior of the Davey-Stewartson II (DSII) system. We demonstrate that the R-knot matrix for DSII exhibits a significance in terms of the wave vector magnitude, $|k|$. Moreover, we establish the invertibility of the R-knot matrix for all admissible values of $|k|$.

This study employs post-Newtonian theory to investigate the residual eccentricity of nearly parabolic falling orbits around a compact object, a property that persists after emitting gravitational waves down to a specific finite eccentricity. We derive both an exact analytical formula and precise numerical values for this residual eccentricity, examining dependencies on the masses and spins of the interacting bodies. Our findings indicate that, for a wide range of initial conditions, the resulting eccentricity falls between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we address the question of whether this value is universal or varies based on the system's initial state.

The High Luminosity Coherent X-ray source (HLX) is a proposed facility designed to deliver high brightness polarization light across a spectrum from 0.1 to 10 keV. This source operates as a soft X-ray Free-Electron Laser (FEL) in an oscillator-regenerative amplifier configuration, utilizing a 2.5 GeV linear accelerator and a 300-meter undulator. The system's oscillator operates in a "fully coherent" mode, where the seed beam perfectly overlaps with the self-amplified spontaneous emission (SASE) within the undulator, a mode noted for generating peak power. In this specific design, a Free-Electron Laser Oscillator (FELO) is positioned at the focus of a mirror to achieve full coherence with SASE. The mirror must possess high reflectivity across 0.1–0.5 keV and maintain angular precision of 100 microradians. The FELO is required to generate a 0.15 keV coherence area of $10^6$ lambda$^2$ with a pulse energy exceeding 10 nanojoules. The amplifier section employs a 0.5-meter tapered undulator driven by a 20 Mega-electronvolt, 200 Amperes electron beam to produce output powers between 10 and 100 kilowatts within a 0.1–0.5 keV range. Accurately identifying incidents within networks is crucial for maintaining security and reliability. While the classic approach treats this as a binary classification problem, the presence of limited labeled data renders traditional supervised learning ineffective. Although unsupervised techniques have been utilized, the complex and varied nature of incidents often leads to a high false-alarm rate. To address this, we introduce **IncidentEvol**, a novel unsupervised framework that leverages the temporal evolution of incidents for more effective identification. The system operates in two phases: first, it clusters incidents based on the time-series characteristics of the network's structure and traffic patterns; second, it employs an evolution-aware approach to detect incidents. Testing across both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that IncidenceEvout surpasses existing methods in detection accuracy, particularly regarding false alarms.

The dynamics of a spherical shock wave penetrating a gaseous medium are modeled using a system of ordinary differential equations that account for variable density and exhibit autonomous characteristics. By applying degree theory for Newton's equations, the existence of periodic solutions is proven, indicating that shocks can periodically collapse to zero velocity and strength within this variable-density gas model. Numerical simulations are presented to explore the solution space, specifically to investigate the conditions under which such shock collapse is avoided entirely.

Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly permeating critical real-world domains, such as healthcare and automotive industries, often prompting concerns regarding their lack of transparency and accountability. Consequently, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged to address these issues by seeking to clarify how black-box models function to enhance system accountability. While existing literature predominantly investigates the technical capabilities of explainers and the algorithms themselves, the perspectives of human users remain underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by examining the specific requirements of end-users, namely patients and doctors, within the context of skin cancer detection. Through the collection and analysis of twelve related research studies, the authors identified and categorized ten distinct patient requirements and six doctor requirements. These user-centric needs were subsequently organized into four overarching categories to define the specifications for an ideal explanatory artifact. Ultimately, the study proposes integrating a requirements engineering phase at the outset of the XAI development lifecycle to better align system outputs with human necessities.

We introduce "UniToPatho," a specialized database containing 1,000 H&E stained and whole-slide image sections of colorectal polyps. The collection features 100 fully annotated high-magnification sections for each of ten distinct classes, accompanied by expert annotations on the distribution of tissue areas. To ensure high-quality labeling, a diverse team of ten expert pathologists contributed to the annotation process using a consensus-based approach to maximize reliability. Furthermore, we provide a detailed segmentation of the normal and abnormal components within the histological samples. The authors hope this resource will significantly benefit researchers in the fields of pathology and computational pathology.

This research investigates source encoding under a constraint of zero distortion, analyzing scenarios where the encoder and decoder operate with varying levels of knowledge about the source distribution. We introduce a novel data leakage metric to source encoding, demonstrating its equivalence to mutual information between the source and an imperfect distribution held by the encoder. By introducing a graph theoretical framework, we establish lower and upper bounds on leakage for quantization and lossless source coding tasks. Furthermore, we detail several experimental outcomes.

We introduce a new deep generative model designed specifically for Super-Resolution of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images. The core architecture relies on a hierarchical framework that utilizes two recurrent neural networks to generate high-resolution outputs from low-resolution inputs. To address the challenge of limited paired SAR datasets, we employ a method to create synthetic training examples by hierarchically downsampling images and applying Gaussian noise to their high-resolution versions as targets for the network. Additionally, to enhance the realism of these generated labels, a patch-level intensity correction technique is applied to align dynamic ranges between corresponding regions. Evaluation against standard super-resolution benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches, achieving superior Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) scores.

We introduce a Bayesian enhancement for the Quantum Approximation Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to mitigate measurement noise, utilizing Bayesian updating to refine parameter estimates based on accumulated experimental data and thereby reducing total annealer usage. Since every QAOA iteration is constrained by costly experimental measurements, our strategy of parameter learning through data aggregation improves solution quality by lowering the total number of QAOV runs required. Furthermore, we address how to effectively integrate this enhancement with various parameter optimization techniques. We evaluate the proposed framework through extensive numerical simulations, including comparisons with other noise reduction strategies, and present an initial experimental test conducted on real quantum hardware.

This paper introduces an algorithm for computing the intersection of two ellipses with arbitrary orientations and sizes. The resulting method produces a set of one or two ellipses (or line segments) that represent the intersection region(s), or indicates if no intersection exists. The approach relies on a root-finding strategy utilizing the characteristic equation of two co-rotating ellipses to determine intersection points. The derived formula for this characteristic equation is new, and the study confirms that all real roots correspond to valid intersections while any complex roots are spurious. The algorithm's validity is verified through a demonstration on an embedded ellipse within another, and a Python implementation is made available on GitHub for users to experiment with.

Adaptive methods for updating machine learning models during their deployment are increasingly vital as data streams evolve over time. Although such online learning has been studied for years, most existing approaches for regression and classification rely on retraining the model from scratch using all accumulated data. This full retraining incurs significant computational costs and often leads to suboptimal performance by disregarding previous learning. To address this, we introduce q-Training in Ongoing Time (QOT), an online learning framework capable of efficiently and effectively updating models with new data batches while retaining historical information. By employing q-approximate gradient descent, QOT provides a robust mechanism for model adaptation. Our experiments, conducted on both synthetic datasets and real-world applications, demonstrate that Qot delivers superior predictive accuracy and lower computational costs compared to standard online learning alternatives.

We investigate electron transport in triangular lattice systems, focusing on interactions and lattice distortions. By employing a Hubbard model that incorporates next-nearest-neighbor hopping ($t'$) and distortion parameters ($\delta$), we utilize density functional theory plus Hubbard projection (DFT+DMFT) to explore the temperature- and momentum-dependent spectral function alongside magnetic order parameters. Our findings reveal that magnetic oscillations emerge in the $q$-$T$ phase diagram, specifically within the antiferromagnetic ordering wavevectors of both $q=(\pi, \pi)$ and $q=(2\pi/3, 2\pi/3)$. We further examine the temperature evolution of the order parameter relative to the $q$-point and identify an "order-by-disorder" mechanism where thermal fluctuations stabilize the $(2\pi/3, 2\pi/3)$ state over the $(\pi, \pi)$ state. Additionally, we analyze the phase diagram in the temperature-distortion plane, observing a transition from the $(\pi, \pi)$ to the $(2\pi/3, 2\pi/3)$ magnetic phase as distortion increases.

Vertebrae play a critical role in spinal disease diagnosis and treatment planning, with spine CT being a primary modality for their recognition. However, clinical practice often faces challenges due to inconsistent vertebral positioning and recognition caused by variations in patient posture and movement. This paper introduces a new Automatic Vertebrae Positioning (AVP) framework, Spine Rectification and Anatomically-constrained Enhancement (SRAE), designed to address these issues. The framework operates in two stages: initially, it utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to locate the center of the intervertebral disc (IVD) for every vertebra; subsequently, an optimization algorithm refines these positions by leveraging the smoothness of the spinal curve. The rectification process reorients the spine to a vertical alignment, thereby standardizing vertebral views. Following this, the method employs another CNN to recognize vertebral classes from the rectified images. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the initial study applying AVP for vertebral recognition in CT scans. Experimental results demonstrate that the SRAE method achieves a 98.1% success rate in vertebral positioning and a 95.1% accuracy in vertebral recognition on a CT dataset.

The application of stochastic calculus of variations to physical systems yields random dynamical systems characterized by stochastic trajectories. These systems serve as a universal framework for modeling diverse phenomena, ranging from the evolution of cosmic structures and climate change to the development of tumors and the spread of pandemics. In this paper, we examine the gauge symmetries inherent in the random dynamical system derived from random thermodynamics. We demonstrate that the asymptical measures associated with these systems remain gauge invariant, a conclusion that relies entirely on a specific weak-stochastic integration rule. This conclusion extends to the second author's prior work on "II," which explores more intricate systems involving non-trivial diffusion.

For a rational vector field $X$ defined on a compact, oriented manifold $M$, we introduce the concept of the relative quantum homology relative to $X$. The history of this notion traces back to works by Ruan and others, who explored it within the framework of relative quantum Gromov-Witten theory. The primary contribution of this paper is the development of an arrow product for this new relative quantum homology and the demonstration of its functorial behavior under diffeomorphisms that fix points on the manifold's boundary.

We present an acoustic analog of the tunnel effect, where a vacuum gap between two piezoelectric crystals allows for the transmission of transmitted acoustic waves. This phenomenon enables the complete transfer of mechanical acoustic waves into electrical signals and back again. This study introduces an innovative optical characterization method for liquid liquid exciton-polariton assemblies within active optical reservoirs. Employing beam propagation analysis, we demonstrate how to determine the mean position and spatial extent of exciton-polariton assemblies. This technique enables the precise measurement of both the density and interaction strength of the liquid droplets. We further validate the applicability of this approach by utilizing it to observe changes in droplet properties caused by variations in temperature and excitation power.

The discovery of an ultra-hot gas giant, K2-22 b, orbiting a young, active K2V star at an extreme distance of 0.015 AU has sparked intense study into the mechanisms of atmospheric erosion. Our new observations utilizing the Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Large Binocular Telescope with their Mid-Infrared Instrument (now named the Multi-Object Spectrograph and Imaging device, though referred to as LBT/MIRI in the source) reveal that the dust-producing exosphere surrounding this planet consists of large particles, with radii exceeding 0.15 µm. These findings indicate a substantial mass loss rate of approximately 10⁹ g/s, a figure roughly 100 times higher than typical values for ultra-hot Jupiters. Our models suggest that atmospheric escape driven by stellar X-ray and Extreme Ultraviolet (XUV) radiation drives the formation of silicate dust grains, which subsequently grow and migrate outward through collisionless drag mechanisms.

A topological space $X$ possesses the *coherence* property if, for every map $f: (X, x_0) \to (Y, y_0)$ from a connected, connected component of $Y$ that is locally contractible and path-connected, the induced map on fundamental groups, $f_*: \pi_1(X, x_0) \to \pi_1(Y, y_0)$, is surjective. This property holds for many spaces encountered in algebraic geometry, including smooth quasi-projective varieties over a field. This paper demonstrates that a smooth quasi-projective variety $V$ over a field $k$ is coherent if and only if its crucial locus is flat.

Binary da ta analysis serves as a crucial technique for uncovering undocumented software components at the various levels of a compilation stack, enabling inverse engineering efforts to identify specific binary features that can then be mapped to corresponding source code elements. This study introduces Daany, an integrated suite of tools designed to examine .NET assemblies by extracting comprehensive metadata and interpreting the .CIL intermediate language. Leveraging this capability, Daany has been employed to investigate large-scale .NET projects, including the .NET runtime itself and the Visual Studio IDE, thereby revealing significant insights into these complex codebases.

This paper examines the evolution of the relationship between mathematics and the humanities during the Scientific Renaissance, a period spanning the late 1500s to the early 1600s. It focuses on the contrasting viewpoints of Galileo and Johannes Keplar, specifically regarding the role of intuition in scientific discovery. While Kepler's background in astrology influenced his belief that intuitive connection to nature was vital for understanding natural laws, this approach faced criticism from the more rigorously logical Galileo. The article highlights how Galileo's rejection of intuition in favor of strict mathematical demonstration created a lasting divide between the two disciplines, a dynamic that continues to shape debates in contemporary philosophy of science.

Saha's theory of ionization is fundamental to cosmology, particularly regarding the primordial Universe and the determination of the Universe's age at the epoch of recombination. This study investigates the ionization history of the primordial cosmos by applying a statistical framework to ionization dynamics, which yields a non-Gaussian extension of the Saha equation. Unlike traditional approaches, this method incorporates ionization history non-Gaussianity, revealing that ionization fraction distributions exhibit significant asymmetry. Consequently, there is a disparity between the ionization fraction predicted by the modified Saha equation and that derived from this new statistical model, a discrepancy that becomes pronounced in the late phase of ionization. Furthermore, the application of the new statistical model to CMB power spectrum analysis indicates that neglecting non-Gaussian influences in ionization fraction calculations can result in biases of approximately 0.001 in the CMB angular power spectrum during large angular scales.

This study introduces a novel hybrid simulation approach combining magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) with Particle-In-Cell (PIC) technology, designed to examine magnetic island coalescence. Unlike traditional methods that employ periodic boundaries, this model utilizes spherical coordinates with dynamically integrated PIC particles to follow fluid elements throughout their entire lifecycle. By synchronizing fluid particles with these embedded particles, the model calculates localized MHD properties within each computational cell. Applied to the magnetic reconnection scenario involving X-point formation, the technique successfully captures island merging with high fidelity. The results reveal that the PIC component provides enhanced resolution of kinetic effects, particularly in the vicinity of the X-point and the magnetic separatrices.

Ammanuensis is an open-source project dedicated to developing a code completion engine capable of understanding the semantic context within a function. It utilizes Transformer-based models trained on a broad spectrum of programming languages, including Python, Java, JavaScript, and more. The system's architecture features a dual-encoder design: one processes the source code to be completed while the other analyzes inline comments for deeper semantic meaning, effectively bridging syntactic structures with underlying logic. To enhance its ability to learn function-level concepts, the project introduces "CodeLlama," a specialized transformer model trained on detailed functional descriptions. Furthermore, the system employs an innovative "trace-guided" completion strategy that uses execution traces to validate predicted code, ensuring high accuracy.
